summaries.example: Imagine a kind ruler choosing between two towns to help. One view says the ruler is free only if she could have chosen either town. Another says she is free if nobody outside her forces her and she understands why one choice is better. Philosophers ask which ideas apply to God.
summaries.summary: Divine freedom is the question of whether God can freely choose and act. The entry describes four main ideas. First, freedom may require real alternatives at the moment of action. Second, freedom may require freedom from outside restraints. Third, a free action may need to respond to reasons, such as what is good or wise. Fourth, God may need to be the deepest source of the action. These ideas do not always fit together easily. For example, if God is perfectly good and always does what is best, does God still have another choice? Philosophers give different answers. The discussion also asks whether there is one best possible world, many equally good worlds, or no best world. It considers how these views affect freedom and whether it makes sense to praise or thank God. The entry presents these disagreements without settling them.
key_ideas: The entry studies whether God can be free and what freedom would mean for a divine being.
Some philosophers say freedom requires being able to do something else. Others say freedom can exist when a person acts wisely and is not externally forced.
Other views focus on acting for good reasons or being the true source of one’s actions.
These questions connect divine freedom with goodness, power, possible worlds, praise, thanks, and arguments about whether God exists.
summaries.why_it_matters: The question matters because ideas about God’s freedom affect how people understand divine goodness, power, responsibility, and action. It also connects with questions about human free will and evil. If freedom requires other choices, always doing the best might seem limiting. If freedom means acting wisely without outside force, always doing the best might look like perfect freedom. Understanding the different meanings helps us discuss religious and philosophical ideas carefully.

important_terms.definition: The ability to guide one’s actions rather than being forced by something else.
A being’s ability to choose or act without an outside force controlling the choice.
A reason that makes one choice seem better or more fitting than another.
Being the deepest source of an action, rather than having the action forced by something else.

questions_to_think_about: Must someone be able to choose differently in order to be free?
Could always choosing the best action still count as freedom?
Is a choice free if nobody forces it but the chooser’s character makes the choice certain?
Why might people want to thank or praise someone for an action?

summaries.example: Suppose an agent chooses between possible worlds. If one world is uniquely best, a reasons-based account may say that selecting it is free because the agent acts on decisive reasons. An alternative-possibilities account asks whether the agent could have selected a worse world. If not, it may deny freedom in that respect, even though the action is rational, unforced, and sourced in the agent.
summaries.summary: The entry examines contemporary philosophical models of divine freedom for a God understood as necessary, omnipotent, omniscient, perfectly good, perfectly rational, and creator and sustainer of contingent reality. It organizes the discussion around four possible conditions. The first is synchronic alternative possibility: at the time of action, God must be able to perform or refrain from the action. The second is independence from external constraints. The third is responsiveness to reasons; on some accounts, God’s perfect rationality makes acting on decisive reasons a form of freedom rather than a limitation. The fourth is ultimate sourcehood or agent causation, according to which God is the source of action in a way not reducible to prior events. These conditions can conflict. Essential moral perfection may remove alternatives involving wrongdoing, while a reasons-based account may regard that limitation as an achievement of perfect freedom. The entry applies the models to the choice of a possible world. A unique best world, several equally good or incomparable unsurpassable worlds, and an infinite hierarchy of improving worlds create different problems. Satisficing—choosing a sufficiently good option rather than the best—offers one response, though its intelligibility is contested. The discussion also considers modal collapse, the appropriateness of divine praise and thanks, and links between divine freedom and arguments for or against theism. The entry maps these positions rather than endorsing one final solution.
key_ideas: The entry uses four proposed conditions for divine freedom: alternative possibilities, no external constraints, responsiveness to reasons, and ultimate sourcehood.

The usual human distinction between compatibilism and incompatibilism does not transfer neatly to God, since divine action is not normally thought to be determined by natural laws. The deeper issue is whether God’s nature, goodness, or rationality determines divine action.

Perfect goodness creates a central tension. If God cannot act wrongly, then an alternative-possibilities theory may say that God lacks an important kind of freedom. Other theories treat flawless goodness as compatible with, or even constitutive of, perfect freedom.

Possible-world cases test the theories. God might face one best world, several unsurpassable worlds, or an endless ranking with no best world. Views involving satisficing allow a good-enough choice rather than the best one, but that proposal is disputed.
Agent-causal accounts make God the ultimate source of action, while critics question whether causation by an agent can be explained without appealing to prior events, states, or reasons.
The debate matters for whether God can properly be praised or thanked, and for arguments concerning divine attributes, human freedom, evil, foreknowledge, and the existence of God.
summaries.why_it_matters: Divine freedom is not an isolated question about a religious attribute. It tests whether a conception of God’s necessary existence, power, knowledge, rationality, and goodness can fit together coherently. It also clarifies what freedom itself might require: alternatives, independence, rational agency, or authorship of action. The results affect debates about moral responsibility, the problem of evil, divine foreknowledge, creation, and whether praise or gratitude toward God is intelligible. Studying the competing models shows why apparently simple claims—such as “God always does what is best”—can generate difficult questions about possibility and agency.

important_terms.definition: The philosophical question of whether God’s will and actions satisfy conditions for freedom.
The view that an action is free only if the agent could have acted otherwise at the time of acting.
The view that freedom can be compatible with an action’s being determined by the agent’s nature or reasons.
The view that freedom is incompatible with relevant determination; divine libertarianism combines this with the claim that God is free.
A condition on freedom requiring that the agent is not compelled or controlled by something external.
A condition on freedom requiring action to be guided by considerations that count in favor of acting.
The view that an agent, rather than merely an event or prior state, is the ultimate source of an action.
The possibility that, on theism, some or all apparent alternatives are not genuinely possible because of God’s necessary nature.

questions_to_think_about: Is the ability to do otherwise necessary for freedom, or can acting from decisive reasons be enough?
If God’s nature guarantees perfect goodness, is God’s action determined in a freedom-undermining way?
Would choosing among equally unsurpassable worlds be rational, random, or an expression of personality?
Does being the ultimate source of an action explain freedom, or merely rename the problem?
Should praise and thanks require that an agent could have acted differently?

summaries.example: Imagine a student choosing a project topic. One theory says the student is free only if she could honestly have chosen a different topic. Another says she is free if no teacher forced her, she understands her reasons, and the choice comes from her. Now imagine that she always picks the most helpful project. Is that perfect self-control, or does it mean she was not really free? Philosophers ask similar questions about God.
summaries.summary: Divine freedom asks whether God can make free choices and what would make those choices free. The entry presents four leading proposals. First, God might need alternative possibilities: when acting, God could have done something else. Second, God might need to be free from external constraints, such as another power forcing the decision. Third, God might need to respond to reasons, understanding what is good and acting on it. Fourth, God might need to be the ultimate source of the action. These proposals sometimes disagree. If God is necessarily and perfectly good, perhaps God cannot choose evil. That seems to remove some alternatives, but defenders of other theories say perfect goodness and perfect rationality may describe the highest kind of freedom. The entry then considers choices among possible worlds. There might be one best world, several equally good or incomparable best worlds, or an endless series in which every world can be improved. Some philosophers say God could choose a good-enough world rather than the best; others question whether that is acceptable or even understandable. The discussion also explores whether eliminating possible alternatives creates modal collapse, and whether freedom is needed for thanking, praising, or worshipping God. These are competing philosophical models, not conclusions the entry treats as settled.
key_ideas: The entry asks what freedom would mean for God, using ideas developed in debates about human free will.
One approach requires God to have been able to do something else. Other approaches say God is free if nothing outside God forces the choice.
Another approach says freedom involves understanding and following good reasons. On this view, always choosing what is best might show perfect freedom.
A fourth approach says God must be the ultimate source of divine actions, not merely the place where earlier events lead to an action.
Different pictures of the best possible world create different challenges for these theories.
The debate connects with whether God can be praised and thanked and with arguments about God’s existence.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic helps us see how one idea can have several meanings. People often connect freedom with choice, independence, good reasons, and responsibility, but those connections can pull in different directions. The debate also asks whether a perfect being can have meaningful choices. It matters for religious views about God’s goodness and power, for arguments about evil and foreknowledge, and for the question of whether praise or gratitude make sense. Comparing the models encourages careful thinking instead of assuming that “free” has only one definition.

important_terms.definition: The ability of a person or being to direct actions rather than being controlled by outside pressure.
The question of whether God can choose and act freely.
A real option that could be selected instead of the action that was chosen.
A force or condition outside the agent that blocks or compels an action.
Acting because one understands what counts in favor of a choice.
Being the main source of an action, rather than having the action caused by another agent.
Choosing an option that is good enough instead of the very best option.
A situation in which choices that seemed possible are ruled out by a necessary feature of reality.

questions_to_think_about: Can someone be free while always choosing the best option?
Does being unforced matter more than having other choices?
If two options are equally good, can choosing either one be rational?
What would happen to freedom if only one possible world remained?
Can someone deserve thanks even when they could not have acted differently?
